tip: 'Qu'est-ce que c'est ?' is the everyday 'what is it?', but it literally stacks up as 'what is it that it is?' French keeps the whole chunk as one set phrase.
French skips the 'do' in questions: 'Pourquoi tu ris ?' is just 'why you laugh' – no helper verb, and the rising tone does the asking.
To ask the date, French asks what day WE are: 'Quel jour sommes-nous ?' is literally 'what day are we?' You answer with 'nous sommes...' too.
French asks what size you MAKE, not wear: 'Quelle taille faites-vous ?' uses faire (to make/do) for clothing and shoe sizes.
That plural -ent ending is silent: 'jouent' sounds exactly like 'joue'. The written third-person plural ending vanishes when spoken.
'Propre' after the noun means clean: 'la chambre est propre'. Move it before the noun and it flips to 'own' – ma propre chambre = my own room.
French doesn't capitalize nationalities used as adjectives: 'italien', not Italien. Capitalize only the noun for a person – un Italien.
Put 'est-ce que' in front of any statement to make it a yes/no question: 'Est-ce que c'est gratuit ?' It literally means 'is it that...' – untranslated filler.
'S'il vous plaît' literally means 'if it pleases you'. The vous is the formal 'you' – with friends it becomes s'il te plaît.
'Toilettes' is always plural in French – hence 'où sont' (where are), never 'où est'. There's no singular une toilette for the room.
For 'what is' plus a noun, French uses 'quelle est', not qu'est-ce que: 'Quelle est ton adresse ?' Quel/quelle agrees with the noun's gender.
French orders food with prendre (to take): 'Qu'est-ce que tu prends ?' means what are you having, literally 'what are you taking?'
Feeling is reflexive in French: 'tu te sens' is literally 'you feel yourself'. The 'te' isn't optional – se sentir always carries it.
'Anniversaire' covers both a birthday and a wedding anniversary – one word for both. Here 'ton anniversaire' is your birthday; context decides.
'Regarder' already means 'look at' – no 'at' follows: 'qu'est-ce que tu regardes'. Adding à or another word for 'at' would be wrong.
French phones TO someone: 'téléphoner à' needs the à – 'je téléphone à la banque'. English drops the preposition, French requires it.
French checks how things GO, not how they are: 'ne va pas' (from aller, to go) is literally 'doesn't go' = is wrong. Ça va ? = does it go?
'Vouloir dire' literally reads 'to want to say', but together it just means 'to mean': 'qu'est-ce que ça veut dire' = what does that mean?
In everyday French, 'on' means 'we': 'où est-ce qu'on se retrouve' = where do we meet? It takes a singular verb even though it means us.
French builds adverbs much like English '-ly', by adding '-ment': lent (slow) becomes 'lentement' (slowly). So 'plus lentement' = more slowly.
French can't strand a preposition at the end: it's 'pour qui est ce cadeau', literally 'for whom is this gift', never a dangling 'for'.
Languages take a definite article in French: you don't learn 'French', you learn 'le français' – hence 'apprends le français'.
'Entrée' here means the entrance. On a menu it's the starter course, never the main dish – English borrowed the word and flipped its meaning.
Flip verb and subject for a polite question: 'Voulez-vous...?' = do you want. The hyphen links them – vous voulez becomes voulez-vous.
'Souvenir' means a memory first, a keepsake second – both from the verb se souvenir (to remember). So 'des souvenirs' can be either.
